sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page says what it is at a glance.** The product name, the page title, the date range and three labelled numbers with their changes tell a first-time viewer this is a 12-week traffic and sign-up dashboard. Nothing on the page needs to be worked out first.
- **It holds together as one piece.** It uses one typeface and one grey and white surface. The same rounded white cards are used for both the numbers and the chart, and all three changes use the same green. Each card keeps its layout: label, then the big number, then the change against the earlier period. Nothing looks borrowed from another system, and every border and card groups something.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **The chart may not add up to the Visits total.** By eye, the three channel lines average about 5.9k (Search), 3.6k (Social) and 1.95k (Email) a week. Over 12 weeks that is about 137k visits, but the Visits card shows 184,220. Either other channels are left out of the chart, or the numbers disagree. A reader who adds them up will doubt one or the other. Check the data. If other channels exist, show an "Other" line or say in the chart title that only the top channels are shown.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

The checklist walk is done and the reference entries are read; here is the report.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start? No.**
   - **Where:** The three KPI numbers "184,220", "3,912" and "2.12%" (cards at x 48–1232, y 142–262) are the same size, weight and colour. Each has the same green delta line under it. "Overview" at (48,105) is almost the same size as the numbers, so it doesn't lead either. The chart (y 282–783) is the biggest thing on the page, but only by area. Inside it, the blue Search line pulls the eye only because it is the highest and most saturated mark.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The eye lands on the KPI row and scans sideways across three equal claims. Nothing tells the viewer which number answers "are we on track?" On a weekly-glance dashboard, that means reading all three and ranking them yourself every time.
   - **Why:** Tschichold, *The New Typography*: show the order of importance by differences of size. Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*: build the composition from "much against little."
   - **Fix:** Decide which metric is the headline for this team, probably sign-ups or conversion rate. Make it clearly first, for example a wider or first-placed card with a larger figure, and set the other two back. If the three really are peers, a common dashboard choice, at least let the page title or the chart lead so the eye has one starting point.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, partly taste, since equal KPI cards are a common and defensible dashboard pattern. Minor.
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same? No.**
   - **Where:** "Overview" (about 24 px bold, cap height about 17 px at y≈97–114) sits directly above the KPI figures (about 28 px bold, cap height about 20 px at y≈192–214).
   - **What the viewer gets:** At a glance the page title and the data read as the same level. The title looks like a slightly smaller fourth number rather than the heading over everything. The size gap is a few pixels with the same weight and colour, which reads as an accident rather than a choice.
   - **A second, smaller collision:** The brand "Brightpath Analytics" (48,28) and the chart title "Visits by channel" (71,313) look like the same size and semibold style. Yet one is app chrome and the other is a section heading.
   - **Why:** Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8: weak contrast is worse than none. Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1: use a modest set of distinct intervals. Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*: two to four levels, each distinct at a glance.
   - **Fix:** Separate "Overview" from the figures in an obvious way. Either make the title clearly larger, or make it clearly quieter (smaller, lighter or grey) and let the numbers be the big type. Give the brand a different treatment from section titles, such as a different weight or colour, or a logo mark.
   - **Not counted as a collision:** The small sizes (labels and legend about 14 px, deltas about 13 px, axis about 12 px) are close together, but colour already tells them apart (grey labels, green deltas, grey axis).
   - **Type and weight:** Defect for the title and number pair (the levels blur). Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Headings use weight, not just size:** Headings and figures differ from the text around them in weight and colour too. The dark bold KPI figures sit over light grey labels and green deltas. The semibold chart title sits over a plain legend. So inside each card the order (label, number, change) reads at once.
- **Chart has a clear grouping:** The chart's title, legend and plot are grouped and ordered top to bottom, so the second level of the page is easy to follow once the eye gets there.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element dominates; distinct text levels with no near-equal sizes), 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

The one place I looked hard was the bottom of the image. The chart card ends at about y=783, only about 17 px above the image edge, while the side margins are 48 px. Seventeen pixels still clears the edge, so it doesn't fail "Content keeps clear of the page edge" (basics.md). It is probably just where the viewport capture was cut (see below). Inside the chart card, the space under the x-axis labels (about 45 px, y≈738 to 783) is about twice the top padding (about 20 px above "Visits by channel"). That's a small unevenness, not a failure on any line here.

**What's working.**
- **One grid, held exactly.** A single left edge at x≈48 runs through "Brightpath Analytics", "Overview", the Visits card and the chart card. A single right edge at x≈1231 runs through "Last 12 weeks", the Conversion rate card and the chart card. The three KPI cards take equal thirds with matching gutters of about 20 px. The gap between the card row and the chart (y≈262 to 282) is the same 20 px. Inside the boxes, the padding is the same too: the KPI labels and "Visits by channel" both sit about 21 px in from their card edges. The page reads as one system, so the eye compares the three numbers at once without fixing any alignment. Keep this when adding cards or rows.
- **The boxes match the groups and the eye has a clear path.** Each card holds one metric: its label, its value, and its change, with the label and the three values on shared baselines across the cards. The chart card holds the title, legend and plot as one unit. The order runs Overview → three numbers → their breakdown over time, top-left to bottom, and nothing leads the eye off the page.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Bottom margin.** If the page scrolls on, or has 48 px of bottom padding below the fold, the bottom margin is fine. If 800 px is the whole page, the chart card sits too close to the bottom edge compared with the 48 px sides. Check this in a live browser.
- **Reflow.** I can't tell from a still how the three-card row stacks at narrower widths.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the three big KPI figures (184,220 / 3,912 / 2.12%), then drops to the blue line in the chart. It reads as a marketing analytics overview for a small team, and it feels calm and generic. Job, assumed: let someone check traffic, sign-ups and conversion over the last 12 weeks at a glance. The image is about 1280×800, a single screen. The crop script could not run because Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image.

Text walk:
- Body text large enough: yes. There is no body text, and labels are about 14 px.
- Captions and labels large enough: yes. Axis ticks are about 11–12 px and delta lines about 13 px, normal for a dashboard.
- Paragraph face: yes (none).
- One typeface plan: yes. It is one sans family throughout.
- Small text weight: yes.
- Contrast on plain background: yes. Grey labels and dark green deltas look comfortably above 4.5:1.
- Text over image: yes (none).
- Line length, leading, multi-line heading, flush left, justified, rag, widows, paragraph marks, hanging punctuation, chunking: yes (none of these occur).
- No all-caps sentences: yes.
- Emphasis changes one thing: yes.
- Large headings tighter: yes. "Overview" is only about 24 px.
- Kerning in large type: yes. The KPI figures look even.
- Lower-case tracking: yes.
- Capitals letterspaced: yes (none).
- Ligatures: yes (none at size).
- Real bold: yes.
- Quotes, dashes and ellipses: yes (none).
- Tabular figures: yes. The y-axis ticks are right-aligned, and there are no number columns.
- Real type: yes.
- Nothing clipped: yes.

All lines are yes, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One family, clear hierarchy.** A single sans is used at a few clear steps: the KPI figures at about 26 px bold, "Overview" at about 24 px bold, card and chart titles at about 16 px semibold, labels at about 14 px, and deltas and axis ticks at about 12 px. Every size has an obvious job, and the step from the grey card labels to the near-black figures is done with weight and colour, not crowded sizes (Refactoring UI). Keep this when adding content.
- **Self-explaining delta lines.** "+6.1% vs previous 12 weeks" gives the change, the unit and the comparison. The conversion card correctly uses "+0.1 pts" rather than "%", so the viewer can't confuse a relative change with an absolute one. Those are the numbers people will quote, and they read only one way.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **A restrained, neutral base.** The page is almost all neutral: a pale gray background (about y 60–800), white cards with thin gray borders, and near-black text. The only saturated colours are the three chart lines (blue, orange, green) and the small green change lines in the cards (+6.1%, +2.4%, +0.1 pts, at about y 234). So colour shows up only where there is data, and the eye goes to the chart and the numbers rather than to decoration (Refactoring UI, on holding back accent colour).
- **Green used for its usual meaning.** The change lines are green, they show improvements, and each one also has a "+" sign and the words "vs previous 12 weeks". The colour backs up the meaning instead of carrying it alone, so a colour-blind viewer reads it the same way (WCAG 1.4.1).

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

A few colour points belong to other sections, so I didn't file them here:
- The series can only be told apart through a legend matched by colour at the top left (y≈344), with no labels on the lines themselves.
- The green Email line can look like "good" next to the green change lines above it.
- The small green change text may be too faint to read easily.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, or logo mark. "Brightpath Analytics" at the top left is set as plain bold text, not a drawn mark. The legend swatches and the lines belong to the chart, so they come under "Charts and data".

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
I critiqued the "Charts and data" section only, working from the whole image (1280×800 is one screen). I edited no files and made no crops. Two numbers on the page don't add up, which no checklist line covers, so I've added them as findings 1 and 2.

**Section.** Charts and data: applies (three summary cards and one line chart, "Visits by channel").

**Findings**
1. **Not a checklist line: the conversion-rate change contradicts the other two cards.** This is in the "Conversion rate" card (≈872–1232, 142–262), on the line "+0.1 pts vs previous 12 weeks".
   - Visits rose 6.1% and sign-ups rose only 2.4%, so the conversion rate must have fallen.
   - Working back: the previous period had ≈173,630 visits and ≈3,820 sign-ups, which is ≈2.20%. The rate went from 2.20% to 2.12%, a change of about −0.08 pts, not +0.1.
   - Anyone who checks the arithmetic stops trusting the whole dashboard. Anyone who doesn't comes away thinking conversion improved, in green, when it got worse.
   - Fix: recompute the delta from the same data as the other cards. If it's negative, show it in a non-positive colour.
   - Defect. Weight: major.

2. **Not a checklist line: the chart's channels don't add up to the Visits total.** My readings of the chart give roughly Search ≈71k, Social ≈44k and Email ≈23k, about 138k in total. The Visits card says 184,220, so roughly 46k (25%) is missing.
   - Either a channel (Direct, Referral, Other) is missing, or one of the two figures is wrong.
   - The viewer will assume the three lines are all the traffic, and their share of each channel will be wrong.
   - Fix: add the missing channel or an "Other" line in grey, or say in the title or caption that the chart shows only these three channels.
   - These are estimates read off a still image. Check them against the data.
   - Defect. Weight: major.

3. **"Is each series label placed at its data rather than in a separate legend?" and "Can each chart's series be told apart without color vision…?"**
   - The legend sits top-left (71–294, y≈344), about 900 px from where the lines end (x≈1185).
   - The only link from a line to its channel is colour. Orange (Social) and green (Email) can look alike to someone with red-green colour blindness. Those viewers can't reliably tell which line is Social and which is Email.
   - The lines never cross and happen to stack in legend order, which helps, but only by luck.
   - Source: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*; WCAG 1.4.1.
   - Fix: put "Search", "Social" and "Email" at the right end of each line, in the line's colour, and drop the legend.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.

4. **"Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?"**
   - The title "Visits by channel" (71, 313) only names the topic. The viewer has to work out the point alone: Search grew about 36% and leads, Social is volatile, Email is small but steady.
   - Fix: give a takeaway title or subtitle, e.g. "Search drove most of the growth".
   - Taste (no approved source; it's common sense on a dashboard read at a glance). Weight: minor.

5. **"Does each chart name what its marks show, with axis values, units, and series labels?"**
   - The y axis (0–8k, x≈95–111) gives no unit or time step. With 12 points it's probably visits per week, but the viewer has to guess. Nothing tells them that the x-axis dates are week starts, or that the last point (≈Sep 22) has no label.
   - Source: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 2; Few, *Show Me the Numbers*.
   - Fix: add "Weekly visits" to the title or the axis.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **Right chart, low noise:** a line chart for 12 weekly points, with the y axis starting at zero, light gridlines and no effects. Almost all the ink is data, so the trends read straight away.
- **Every headline number has a comparison:** each card states its change against the previous 12 weeks, which is what makes a summary card useful. That's why the conversion error in finding 1 matters so much.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 12 yes, 4 no (series told apart without colour; labels at the data; units named; title states the finding).

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only likely control is "Last 12 weeks" at the top right, which is probably the period picker. The legend might also act as series toggles. There are no buttons, forms or navigation.

**Findings**
1. *Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?*
   - **Where:** "Last 12 weeks" in the header, at about x 1133–1232, y 20–38.
   - **What the viewer meets:** It is set as plain grey text at body size, with no chevron, border, fill or calendar icon, so it reads as a caption describing the data. On an analytics dashboard, changing the period is the most common thing a user does. A user who wants last quarter or last week won't see that this text is the way in, and will look for a control that doesn't seem to exist.
   - **Why:** Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, on affordances and signifiers. NN/g, Moran, "Flat UI Elements Attract Less Attention and Cause Uncertainty" (2017), on clickable text styled as static text.
   - **Fix:** Give it the shape of a control: an outlined or lightly filled button with a chevron, and ideally a calendar icon. Showing the actual dates (e.g. "Jul 7 – Sep 28") in or under it would also help. If it really is only a label, this finding falls away and finding 2 gets heavier.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect if it's a control. Major.
2. *Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?*
   - **Where:** The whole screen. There is no channel filter, no way to compare periods, no drill-down from the KPI cards (y 142–262), and no export.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The user can read the numbers but not question them. Asking "why did Social dip on Jul 21?" or "which channel drove the sign-ups?" means leaving the screen.
   - **Why:** Nielsen, heuristic 7, flexibility and efficiency of use. Some of this may exist as hover or click behaviour that a still can't show.
   - **Fix:** Show at least the frequent ones. Make the KPI cards and legend items visibly clickable to filter or drill down, and put a compare or segment control next to the period picker.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention. Minor.
3. *Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?*
   - **Where:** The "Overview" heading at x 48, y 90–118, and the header bar at y 0–59, which holds only the product name and the period.
   - **What the viewer meets:** "Overview" implies there are other, more detailed views, but there's no navigation to them. A first-time user can't tell whether this one screen is the whole product or how to get deeper.
   - **Why:** Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, ch. 2, on the conceptual model.
   - **Fix:** If other views exist, add navigation (tabs under the header or a side rail) with "Overview" marked as current. If this really is the only screen, rename the heading so it doesn't promise siblings.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect if other views exist, taste if not. Minor.

**What's working.**
- The period control sits in the global header, top right, above everything it governs, which matches where dashboard users expect a date range to be (Jakob's law). Only its styling needs fixing.
- The cards say what each delta is compared with ("vs previous 12 weeks"), and the conversion change is given in "pts", not as an ambiguous percent. The user doesn't have to remember the baseline from somewhere else.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether "Last 12 weeks" and the legend items are interactive at all, and what their hover, focus and pressed states look like.
- Whether the chart shows a tooltip on hover with exact weekly values. That matters here because the y-axis only gives 2k steps.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (controls look like what they do; shortcuts for frequent actions; conceptual model), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).
